title: A pricing page for a logistics company
metaTitle: Logistics pricing page: show the shape
excerpt: Operators use the pricing page to judge fit. Show what the rate includes, which accessorials it does not, and how to request a quote. Do not hide a shape they will ask for anyway.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky, a clear structure for a rate that should be equally legible.
caption: A white modernist building of stacked cubic volumes. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs at the top of a logistics pricing page?
faqs.answer: Put the shape of the rate first: mode, what a standard dock-to-dock move includes, and the minimum if you have one. A worked example in pallets, pounds, and cities helps more than a company history. Visitors read only part of the page, so the part nearest the rate has to carry the deal.

faqs.question: How should accessorials be listed?
faqs.answer: Name them the way an invoice will name them, and say when each one starts. Liftgate, residential, detention, reweigh, and a second attempt are the usual surprises. "May apply" is not a rule. A free window with a clock is a rule an operator can plan around.

faqs.question: What if every lane is a custom quote?
faqs.answer: You can still publish the shape. Say which details you need, what you refuse, and when a number comes back. A minimum and a list of exclusions let someone judge fit before they write. A calculator that collects a long form and then only emails sales is not a rate.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The logistics company pricing page is where an operator decides whether you fit the freight, before they bother with a spreadsheet. Show what the price includes, what it does not, and how to request a quote. If they will ask the shape anyway, publish the shape.

A rate is rarely one number for every load. That is not a reason to publish nothing. Operators have been surprised by the line after the line. Your page can be the place that surprise is written down.

## Fit before arithmetic

The operator arrives with a lane, a ready date, and a guess about weight. They want to know whether you are even the right desk. Mode, region, minimum, and the fees that always appear. If those are clear, they will send the details. If they are not, they will send the details to someone else and let you wonder why the inbox is quiet.

Nielsen Norman Group notes that visitors have time to read only about a quarter of the text on a page they open. On a pricing page, assume the quarter nearest the rate is the quarter they will see. Put the shape there. A history of the company above the rate is the paragraph that gets skipped, or the only paragraph that loads in their attention, and it prices nothing.

Lead with the work you want more of. If standard dry van in a region is the business, price that world first. Do not open with the rare project move because it photographs well. The operator with a Tuesday pickup of eight pallets will not recognize themselves, and they are the one who can say yes this week.

Say who the page is for. The person paying the invoice, not a broker collecting a margin you did not explain, unless brokers are truly who you sell to. If both, give them separate blocks with separate words. A broker reading a shipper's all-in rate, or a shipper reading a broker's buy rate, will feel misled even when the math is honest.

## What the price includes

"Included" means the moves a dispatcher would not add a charge for. Linehaul between the points you named. A standard dock-to-dock pickup. One delivery attempt on an appointment you agreed. The POD. A tracking update at the points you actually update, not a fantasy of minute-by-minute GPS if you do not have it.

Write the assumptions in the units on the bill of lading. Business addresses with a dock. Freight that fits the equipment. A weight you will honor within a stated tolerance before a reweigh. Class or description accurate enough to rate.

If fuel is indexed, say the index in plain language and where to see the current figure. "Fuel follows the weekly surcharge we publish here" is a shape. "Fuel may apply" is a shrug. Operators know fuel moves. They are checking whether you will invent the move in the invoice.

A worked example does more than a definition. "Eight pallets, 4,000 pounds, dock to dock, Chicago to Atlanta, standard transit. The rate includes one pickup and one delivery. It does not include a liftgate or inside delivery." Use a figure you would actually quote, or label the figure as an illustration and keep the inclusions true. A flattering example is a future dispute.

## What the price does not include

This is the section that earns the page. List the accessorials an operator has been burned by, in their names.

Liftgate. Inside delivery. Residential. Limited access, including schools, farms, and job sites if that is how you bill them. Detention after a stated free window. Layover. Reweigh and reclass. A second attempt. Storage when the receiver will not take the freight. Hazardous material, if you touch it at all.

For each one, say when it triggers. "Detention starts after 60 minutes past the appointment, billed in 15-minute increments" is a rule they can plan. "Detention may apply" is the rule they will assume is abusive.

Say what you need in order not to charge the surprise. A call ahead. A photo of the freight. An accurate piece count. The page is allowed to be a little stern. Stern and predictable beats friendly and inventive.

Google's guidance on title links asks the page title to describe the page, without a repeated slogan doing the work. "Accessorials and rates" tells an operator, and a search result, what the page is. "Transparent partnership pricing" could belong to a software company. Use the plain title, and use the same plainness in the headings. The exclusions should look like a tariff a dispatcher could read, not like a brand campaign.

## Show the shape when the lane changes

Most logistics prices move with distance, weight, class, and the day. Hiding all of that behind "contact us for a custom quote" wastes the visit of anyone with a standard shipment. They will ask anyway. Answer with the shape.

A rate card for zones you run often. A minimum charge. A per-mile or per-hundredweight pattern. A note that project freight is quoted from the details, with the list of details and the hour you answer. Any one of these lets a fit decision happen on the page.

If a human must price it, say what they need and when the number returns. Origin, destination, ready date, weight, dimensions, and a description. Same day before a named cutoff. Next morning if it is a mode you run less often. That is still a price page. A form that ends in "a specialist will reach out" with no clock is a lead form wearing a rate sheet's clothes.

Do not build a calculator that collects twelve fields and then emails the sales team. Either the calculator returns a range you will honor for a stated number of days, or it is theater. Theater is how operators lose an afternoon and how your desk inherits bad will.

The quote button on this page uses the same sentence as the homepage. The fields can be prefilled if they came from a lane page. Do not make them retell the shipment in a blank box labeled "message."

## Minimums, credits, and the invoice

Publish the minimum. A small shipment that prices below your cost will be declined or bumped to a minimum charge. Say which. Operators would rather know than discover it as a line called "adjustment."

If you offer a credit for a miss, define the miss. A missed appointment you caused. A transit day you published and did not meet. Say what the credit is, and what it is not. It is not an admission that covers weather you named in the terms, and it is not a vague "service failure" they have to negotiate from zero.

Payment terms belong here too, in one line. Net days, from what document, and what happens to a disputed accessorial. "We will pause the disputed line and collect the rest" is a fit signal for a careful accounts payable team. "Pay the invoice to keep your account in good standing" with no dispute path is a threat, and it will be read as one.

Claims can be a short block or a link to the claims page. Time window, what evidence you need, who decides. Do not hide the window inside a PDF with a different number than the page. The page the operator reads is the page they will cite.

## Keep the quote path attached to the rules

Repeat the request under the inclusions and under the exclusions. A person who has just learned you charge for limited access is exactly the person ready to send accurate details. Do not make them scroll back to a hero button that has floated away.

Tell them what they get back. A rate, an expiration, and the assumptions. "The quote holds for seven days if the weight and the addresses hold." If the quote is a conversation, say that the first reply will be questions, not a number, and list the questions. Surprise questions feel like a stall. Listed questions feel like a desk that knows the work.

If some freight is refused at the quote, say so before they type. You do not haul household goods. You do not quote produce. You do not serve that state. A fast no is a service. It returns the operator to their day and keeps your estimators on loads you can run.

## Read the page like an invoice

Print a recent invoice next to the draft. Every line that appeared on the invoice and surprised someone should be a heading, or a row, on the page. If the invoice has a code the page does not translate, translate it. Operators should not need a glossary call to learn what they already paid.

Then read the page like a new coordinator who has fifteen minutes and a load that must leave tomorrow. Mark every sentence that does not help them decide to send details or to go elsewhere. The unmarked sentences are the page. The marked ones are how pricing pages grow back into brochures.

Check the numbers against the desk before you publish, and again when fuel or a free-time rule changes. A beautiful layout of last year's detention window is a false rate. The person who updates the tariff has to be able to update the page without a project. If they cannot, the page will drift, and the drift will show up as a dispute.

The page beside this one should say what work those rates buy, in the operator's words, including the boundary. That is [the services page a logistics company actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-logistics-company-actually-needs).

If you want to pressure-test which charges belong on the page before you design it, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
